title: Variadic Templates and Fold Expressions
summary: A **variadic template** accepts any number of arguments of any types, written `template <typename... Args>`. The arguments form a **parameter pack**, which you expand with `args...`. **Fold expressions** apply an operator across a whole pack in one expression.
markdown:
## Parameter packs ```cpp #include template void count(const Args&... args) { std::cout << sizeof...(args) << " arguments:"; ((std::cout << ' ' << args), ...); // explained below std::cout << '\n'; } int main() { count(); // 0 arguments: count(1, "hi", 3.5); // 3 arguments: 1 hi 3.5 return 0; } ``` | Syntax | Name | Holds | |---|---|---| | `typename... Args` | A template parameter pack | Zero or more **types** | | `const Args&... args` | A function parameter pack | Zero or more **values**, one of each type | | `sizeof...(args)` | | The number of elements, as a compile-time constant | | `args...` | A pack expansion | The elements, separated by commas | For `count(1, "hi", 3.5)`, `Args` is `int, const char*, double`. A pack is not a container. You cannot index it or loop over it at run time. It can only be **expanded**, and the expansion happens entirely during compilation. This is the type-safe replacement for the C-style `...` in [[5.10 Function Pointers, Callbacks and Command-Line Arguments]]. ## Fold expressions A **fold expression** combines every element of a pack with a binary operator. ```cpp #include template auto sum(Ts... xs) { return (xs + ...); } template void printAll(const Ts&... xs) { ((std::cout << xs << ' '), ...); std::cout << '\n'; } int main() { std::cout << sum(1, 2, 3, 4) << '\n'; // 10 printAll(1, "two", 3.0, 'x'); // 1 two 3 x return 0; } ``` The parentheses around a fold are required. | Form | Name | Expansion for a pack `p1, p2, p3` | |---|---|---| | `(pack op ...)` | Unary right fold | `p1 op (p2 op p3)` | | `(... op pack)` | Unary left fold | `(p1 op p2) op p3` | | `(pack op ... op init)` | Binary right fold | `p1 op (p2 op (p3 op init))` | | `(init op ... op pack)` | Binary left fold | `((init op p1) op p2) op p3` | Left or right matters for operators that are not associative. With the pack `10, 3, 2`: ``` (... - xs) is (10 - 3) - 2 = 5 (xs - ...) is 10 - (3 - 2) = 9 ``` > [!warning] Empty packs > A unary fold over an **empty** pack is an error for most operators. (Only `&&`, `||` and the comma operator have defined results: `true`, `false` and nothing.) Use a binary fold with an initial value when the pack may be empty: `(xs + ... + 0)`. ### The comma fold `printAll` folds over the **comma operator**: `((std::cout << xs << ' '), ...)`. The pattern inside the inner parentheses is repeated for each element, in order. This is the general way to "do something for every argument". ### Useful folds ```cpp template bool allTrue(Ts... values) { return (values && ...); } template bool anyTrue(Ts... values) { return (values || ...); } template bool isOneOf(const T& value, const Ts&... options) { return ((value == options) || ...); } isOneOf(command, "quit", "exit", "q"); ``` In `isOneOf`, the pattern `(value == options)` is expanded once per option, and `||` short-circuits as usual. ## The older technique: recursion Before C++17, a pack was processed by peeling off one argument at a time. ```cpp void print() { std::cout << '\n'; } template void print(const T& first, const Rest&... rest) { std::cout << first << ' '; print(rest...); } ``` ```mermaid flowchart LR A["print(1, 'a', 2.5)"] --> B["prints 1
calls print('a', 2.5)"] --> C["prints a
calls print(2.5)"] --> D["prints 2.5
calls print()"] --> E["new line"] ``` Each step instantiates a new function with one fewer parameter, until the non-template overload with no parameters ends the chain. It is recursion in form only: every "call" is to a different function, and they are usually all inlined. `if constexpr` removes the need for a separate base case: ```cpp template void print2(const T& first, const Rest&... rest) { std::cout << first << ' '; if constexpr (sizeof...(rest) > 0) { print2(rest...); } } ``` `if constexpr` is evaluated during compilation, and the branch not taken is **discarded**: it is not instantiated at all. Without that, `print2()` with no arguments would have to exist. Prefer a fold where one fits; use recursion when each step depends on the previous one. ## Forwarding a pack A wrapper that passes its arguments straight on to another function, as `std::make_unique` does, expands a pack through `std::forward`: ```cpp template std::unique_ptr makeIt(Args&&... args) { return std::unique_ptr(new T(std::forward(args)...)); } ``` The expansion `std::forward(args)...` applies the pattern to each element in step, pairing each type with its value. What `Args&&` and `std::forward` achieve is the subject of [[11.01 Value Categories and Perfect Forwarding]]. ## Variadic class templates Classes can be variadic too. `std::tuple` and `std::variant` are the two you will use most: [[10.04 stdoptional, stdvariant, stdany and stdtuple]]. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What does `sizeof...(args)` give? - The total size in bytes of all the arguments + The number of elements in the parameter pack, as a compile-time constant - The size of the largest argument - The number of template parameters, including non-packs > `sizeof...` counts the elements of a pack. It has nothing to do with bytes. ? Expand `(... - xs)` for the pack 10, 3, 2. + `(10 - 3) - 2`, which is 5 - `10 - (3 - 2)`, which is 9 - `2 - 3 - 10`, which is -11 - `-(10 + 3 + 2)`, which is -15 > With the `...` on the left it is a left fold, grouping from the left. `(xs - ...)` would be the right fold giving 9. ? Why use `(xs + ... + 0)` instead of `(xs + ...)`? - To make the result an `int` - Because `(xs + ...)` adds the elements twice + `(xs + ...)` does not compile for an empty pack - It is only a matter of style > Only `&&`, `||` and `,` have a value for empty packs. The `+ 0` gives the fold a starting value. ? What does `if constexpr` do with the branch that is not taken? - It runs it anyway, then discards the result - It reports a compile error - It moves it to run time + It discards it at compile time, so that branch is never instantiated > Inside a template, the discarded branch can contain code that would not compile for this type. ```
ideas:
1. Write `average(xs...)` returning a `double`, using a fold and `sizeof...`.
2. Write `maxOf(a, b, c, ...)` for any count of at least one.
3. Write `pushAll(vec, xs...)` that pushes every argument into a vector with a comma fold.

cards.a:
The number of elements in the parameter pack, as a compile-time constant

`sizeof...` counts the elements of a pack. It has nothing to do with bytes.

`(10 - 3) - 2`, which is 5

With the `...` on the left it is a left fold, grouping from the left. `(xs - ...)` would be the right fold giving 9.

`(xs + ...)` does not compile for an empty pack

Only `&&`, `||` and `,` have a value for empty packs. The `+ 0` gives the fold a starting value.

cards.q: What does `if constexpr` do with the branch that is not taken?
cards.a:
It discards it at compile time, so that branch is never instantiated

Inside a template, the discarded branch can contain code that would not compile for this type.
